TheEuropean Monitoring Center for Drugs and Drug Addictionreports that England and Wales have the highest marijuana use rate in the EU.

But it gets even better.

In the ranking of the various countries’ " proportion of problem drug users " the EMCDDA says, " Luxembourg appears to have the highest proportion of problem drug users – around seven per thousand population aged 15 to 64. Next come Italy (around six per thousand), the UK and Spain (around five), Ireland and France (around four) and Austria, Belgium and Denmark, (around three) Finland, Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden have the lowest proportion: around two per thousand. "

In a statement that should be the death knell for marijuana prohibition, the agency says, " These rates suggest little direct association between prevalence of problem drug use and national drug policies. Countries have similar, often moderate, levels whether their policies veer to the liberal or restrictive. "

In short, there is no justification for marijuana prohibition. The Netherlands, which allows the sale of marijuana to persons over 18, has a lower marijuana use rate than the very prohibitionist UK, and has a rate of " problem drug users " comparable to very prohibitionist Sweden. In fact, the Swedes have a much higher rate of drug deaths than Holland, which has the lowest such rate in the EU. Deaths due to drug abuse in Sweden are amongst the highest in Europe, having risen from 50 per year in 1970 to 250 per year today. In the age group 20-39, drugs account for 10 percent of all deaths, as many as die in traffic accidents.

From The Daily Telegraph
By Liz Lightfoot, Education Correspondent
http://www.telegraph.co.uk

British are EU's biggest users of cannabis

ENGLAND and Wales are the drug " capitals " of the European Union, with more cannabis users than any other member state.

Nearly one in 10 adults admits having taken cannabis within the previous 12 months, the highest in the EU. Britain also has the largest number of young users, with two in five 15- and 16-year-olds saying they have experimented.

The EU drugs agency in Lisbon, which carried out the survey, said cannabis was the widest available and most commonly used drug in the EU. Its report, published yesterday, added fuel to the row over plans by Ann Widdecombe, shadow home secretary, to give police the powers to issue fixed penalty fines to cannabis users.

Eight members of the shadow cabinet have confessed to having experimented with the drug in their youth. Tim Yeo, agricultural spokesman, caused fresh embarrassment for the Tory leadership when he went on to defend the drug, saying it was " much pleasanter than having too much to drink ".
(MarijuanaNews note: The links are to Telegraph stories.)

EU scrutiny of drug use suggested that only Denmark rivalled Britain for cannabis use. Among 15- and 16-year-olds 24.4 per cent had tried it, compared with 37.5 per cent in England and Wales. Over the previous 12 months, nine per cent of British adults and 23 per cent of 16 to 29-year-olds said they had used cannabis. In Denmark it was 3.3 and six per cent respectively.

Spain had the second highest usage, 7.6 per cent of adults, followed by 5.2 in Holland, 4.7 in France, 4.5 in Germany, 4.4 in Greece, 1.9 in Finland and 1.5 in Belgium and one per cent in Sweden.
See

Curiosity is the usual motive for the younger age group trying the drug, said the drugs agency. " Use is more experimental or intermittent than persistent. "

Amphetamines and ecstasy are the EU's second most commonly used drugs, although ecstasy use is stabilising and even falling, following rises in the Nineties.

At least 45 million Europeans - 18 per cent of the age group 15 to 64 - have tried cannabis once.(Lifetime prevalence)

Experience among schoolchildren ranged from seven per cent in Portugal and Sweden to nearly 40 per cent in Holland, Ireland and Britain.

TORIES' POLICY ON DRUGS IS `MAD', SAYS STRAW

BRITAIN: The British Home Secretary, Mr Jack Straw, said yesterday the Tories' proposed zero tolerance drugs policy was " mad " but he insisted political programmes should never be led by whether or not politicians had indulged in youthful high-jinks.

Mr Straw said the zero tolerance proposal announced by the shadow home secretary, Ms Ann Widdecombe, at the Conservative party conference last week then dropped by the party leader, Mr William Hague, on Monday, was " mad " because it did not recognise the proportionate damage caused by different illegal drugs.

That is not their area of expertise. In fact, if he will check any logic textbook he will find that citing an expert outside of his area of expertise is listed as a classic logical fallacy. What is the opinion of " pharmacologists and psychiatrists " on tax policy? The real public policy debate must be about marijuana prohibition, not about marijuana. That is something that a psychiatrist could address with authority.)

The medical use of cannabis compounds to alleviate symptoms of conditions such as multiple sclerosis, however, could be permitted if medical trials currently underway proved they were beneficial.
